1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Kestrel Bay Regional Hospital (fictional). Unit 5 East is a 20-bed adult ICU with four pods of five beds (Pod A beds 1-5, Pod B 6-10, Pod C 11-15, Pod D 16-20). Bedside monitors sound locally, report to a central station, and send alarms through a clinical alert relay server to nurses' handheld phones. Analysis date: 17 November 2026.
9	Your request: The Chief Nursing Officer asks: why have delayed alarm response incidents on 5 East risen since August, and should she approve the Director of Critical Care Nursing's proposal to cap agency nurse use and open performance reviews for the nurses involved?
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Email from the Director of Critical Care Nursing to the CNO, 3 November (leadership-account): Subject: 5 East alarm incidents, proposal. Delayed alarm response incidents have roughly quadrupled since the summer. The obvious change is staffing. The Larkfield agency contract went live on 5 August, and since then we have had a steady flow of nurses who don't know our pods, plus four new graduates from 1 September. Two of the September incidents involved agency nurses who went to the wrong room. I'm asking for approval to cap agency use at 10% of RN shifts from December and to open performance reviews for every nurse named in a delayed-response report. Our nurses need to know this is being taken seriously.
12	- Incident reporting system extract, category 'alarm response delayed >2 min or not acknowledged', 5 East (system-record): Monthly counts: May 5, Jun 6, Jul 6, Aug 16, Sep 24, Oct 26. Weekly view: 1-2 per week up to and including the week beginning 3 August; 4 in the week beginning 10 August; 5-7 every week from then to 31 October, with no further step change. Harm grading: three moderate-harm events (9 Sep, 3 Oct, 22 Oct); the rest no or low harm. Patient-days per month ranged 588-614 across May-October. The charge nurse usually files the report, and each report names the nurse assigned to the patient.
13	- Nursing workforce report, 5 East, prepared by the finance business partner (financial-record): RN shifts filled by agency: Jun 7%, Jul 8%, Aug 14%, Sep 21%, Oct 24%. Core RN sick leave (% of rostered hours): Jun 3.0, Jul 3.2, Aug 3.4, Sep 6.1, Oct 6.9. Hospital-wide nursing sick leave over the same months rose from 3.1 to 4.4. Resignations: one in September, one in October. Note: the Larkfield contract started 5 August to cover summer annual leave; from September, agency shifts also backfilled sick leave and the two vacancies. Occupational Health bulletin, 28 August: an early respiratory virus season is under way and staff absence is rising across the hospital.
14	- Night charge nurse's huddle notes, 5 East, 2 October (staff-account): Raised at huddle: 'The phones haven't stopped since the summer. I get the same desat three times and by the time I look the sats are back to 96.' 'I've started glancing at the phone instead of reading it.' Agency RN: 'At my other ICU the phones are much quieter for the same kind of patients.' 'Room 14: sometimes my phone doesn't ring at all and I hear the bedside alarm first.' Pod D nurses said they hadn't really noticed a difference. Reminder given: the central station is unstaffed most nights; for rooms you are not in, the phone is how you hear an alarm.
15	- IT service notice and closure note, clinical alert relay (change-record): Notice, 9 August: 'The clinical alert relay server, which forwards bedside monitor alarms to nurse phones, will move to new hardware on 12 August, 01:00-03:00. This is a like-for-like refresh. No user-facing changes are expected. Bedside monitors and the central station are not affected.' Closure note, 12 August 03:40: 'Completed successfully. Configuration imported. Smoke test passed: test alarms from beds 1 and 6 delivered to phones within 3 seconds. No incidents logged.'
16	- Email from the ICU medical director to the CNO, 7 October (expert-account): Before we pin this on the nurses: our case mix has been heavier this autumn, with more cardiac surgery overflow and more patients on high-flow oxygen, so I'm not surprised alarms are up. Also, Biomedical Engineering installed the monitor vendor's software update (v7.2) on all 20 bedside monitors on 23-24 September, and the vendor says it changes how SpO2 problems are alarmed. I'd want both looked at before anyone is disciplined.
17	
18	BRIEF:
19	The rise in delayed alarm responses is most likely caused by the 12 August relay server hardware move, not by agency nurses. The import skipped 11 of 14 forwarding rules. Those rules held back brief SpO2 alarms, suppressed repeat notifications and sent probe-off alarms only to the charge phone. Pods A-C now send about twice as many phone alerts per nurse (about 80 against 38 per shift), and acknowledgement times doubled. Pod D, still on the old server, is unchanged. Within Pods A-C, core, agency and new-graduate nurses all show the same rise, so staffing mix does not explain it. Bedside alarm counts were flat, which argues against heavier acuity and against the monitor software update. The likely mechanism is alarm fatigue. The higher sick leave is only loosely linked to the alert load. Wireless gaps are not excluded, but the pod pattern does not need them. I'm fairly confident, about 85-90%. Next steps: restore the 11 rules after Clinical Engineering validation, as in A1, and track phone alerts per nurse and acknowledgement times weekly. Do not approve the agency cap or the performance reviews. They would punish the wrong people and discourage reporting. Do not switch off SpO2 forwarding to phones.
20
